title: Top civil servant in N.L. fisheries department also travelled on aquaculture company’s dime
summary: Newfoundland and Labrador’s fisheries minister wasn’t the only representative from the provincial government to take part in a study trip in Scotland paid entirely by the aquaculture giant MOWI. His…

image.caption: Long-time seafood industry leader Keith Sullivan was named deputy minister of the Department of Fisheries and Aquaculture last February. Last September, he took a sponsored trip to Scottish aquaculture sites alongside Fisheries Minister Loyola O'Driscoll. (Submitted by Keith Sullivan)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

Newfoundland and Labrador’s fisheries minister wasn’t the only representative from the provincial government to take part in a study trip in Scotland paid entirely by the aquaculture giant MOWI. His department's top civil servant, Keith Sullivan, also tagged along.
Minister Loyola O’Driscoll wasn’t the only representative of province on trip sponsored by MOWI
Newfoundland and Labrador’s fisheries minister wasn’t the only representative from the provincial government to take part in a study trip in Scotland paid entirely by the aquaculture giant MOWI.

Loyola O’Driscoll revealed Monday that his deputy minister, Keith Sullivan, also took part in the sponsored trip, during which both men stayed in a castle and then in a “luxury” shooting lodge — all on the aquaculture company’s dime.

items: N.L. fisheries minister stayed in Scottish castle, ‘luxury’ shooting lodge on aquaculture giant’s dime

blocks.text: Keith Sullivan served as president of the Fish, Food & Allied Workers-Unifor union, then as executive director of the Newfoundland and Labrador Aquaculture Industry Association, before becoming the top civil servant at the Department of Fisheries and Aquaculture last February.
“He also had a clearance, as well,” said O’Driscoll on Monday, noting that the trip was authorized by provincial Legislative Standards Commissioner, Ann Chafe, prior to the duo’s departure.
Newfoundland and Labrador Fisheries and Aquaculture Minister Loyola O'Driscoll speaks to reporters outside the House of Assembly on Nov. 24, 2026. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)
“What do you want me to do? Go back and ask her to double check it again? I certainly got my approval.”
Opposition not satisfied
Despite the commissioner’s decision, both the province’s opposition parties are calling out what they consider a flagrant conflict of interest.

During question period Monday, the NDP bemoaned the leniency of the rules governing gifts and benefits given by companies to elected officials and called for the creation of a new ethics commissioner for the House of Assembly.

Most of the costs for O'Driscoll and Sullivan’s trip to Scotland for the Aquaculture U.K. conference — including airfare and hotel rooms at the beginning and end of the trip — were paid for by the provincial government. However, MOWI organized and paid for travel to several remote aquaculture sites and for the pair’s accommodations between June 16 and 18.
Fisheries and Aquaculture Minister Loyola O'Driscoll holds a salmon during a sponsored trip to MOWI fish farms in Scotland. (Department of Fisheries and Aquaculture)
“If he was there for departmental reasons, why didn't the department pay for it?” asked Liberal fisheries critic Michael King in the House Monday.

“The minister is responsible for regulating the industry,” King said. “He should meet with the stakeholders, but he should not be accepting free accommodations in luxury castles. How does the minister explain to the public that this is acceptable and not create at a minimum the perception of a conflict of interest?”
‘I cannot even believe that we are debating this’
Memorial University political scientist Kelly Blidook called O’Driscoll’s decision and subsequent explanations an “embarrassment.”

“He’s the fisheries minister and he's accepting a benefit from a fish products company. If the rules did allow for this then the rules have to change,” he said. “I cannot even believe that we are debating this.”

Blidook also said that while O’Driscoll and the commissioner of legislative standards contend that all the proper procedures were followed, the minister himself admitted in an interview to Radio-Canada that he had “no idea what the accommodations were” before his trip.
Memorial University politics professor Kelly Blidook. (Submitted by Kelly Blidook)
He questions how Chafe could have made a proper determination on the trip without that information. Chafe refused to grant an interview last week.

Blidook also said it’s “mindblowing” that the financial disclosure addendum signed by the minister after his trip — a public document that’s supposed to outline the source and reasons behind a gift or benefit received by an MHA — can only be viewed in person.
Despite the rules set out in the House of Assembly Act, O'Driscoll's addendum listed neither the value of the sponsored nor the company who paid for it.
“To me, it’s nothing short of mindblowing that the practice is to require individuals to go to the commissioner’s office,” said Blidook.
“It clearly disadvantages the vast majority of Newfoundlanders and Labradorians in terms of access. The whole thing suggests an effort to be as opaque as possible to satisfy the law.”
